opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most interesting shifts happening right now. For a long time, AI research was purely a human craft. You had researchers with intuition who designed architectures, tuned hyperparameters, and cleaned data by hand. Now the models themselves are becoming real participants in that process.

The most immediate way is in engineering. A lot of what slows a team down isn't the big ideas but the plumbing: writing training infrastructure, debugging distributed systems, building evaluation pipelines. Models are already very good at accelerating that. When the iteration loop gets shorter, you can run more experiments, and in this field the number of high-quality experiments you can run is close to the number of things you can learn.

The second way is data. I've always believed that data is something you design, not just something you collect. Models can help generate, filter, and verify data, especially in domains where answers can be checked, like math or code. That creates a kind of flywheel. A stronger model produces better data, which trains an even stronger model. You have to be careful, because if you just feed a model its own outputs without good verification, you get collapse rather than improvement. So the key is building good reward signals and good verifiers.

The third way, which I find the most exciting but which is still early, is AI doing research itself: proposing hypotheses, designing experiments, reading results, and deciding what to try next. Once agents can work reliably over long horizons, they can explore a much larger space than a human team. Humans would then spend more time choosing directions and judging what really matters.

So I'd describe it as climbing a mountain where the tools you use get better the higher you go. That's exciting, but it also means the gap between teams that use this leverage well and teams that don't can widen very quickly. For us, the question isn't whether to use AI to build AI. It's how deeply we can build our whole research organization around it.

r001.rationale: The response says models can accelerate engineering and data work, but it does not state that AI removes lack of coding ability as a barrier to training models or processing data.

fable-5.1.text:
That's actually something I think about a lot, because it's the recursive part of this whole thing. If AI is the most important technology, then the most important application of AI is using it to build better AI.

Right now, in practice, it shows up in a few concrete ways. The most obvious one is coding. A large fraction of the code our team writes now is written with the model in the loop. Infrastructure, data pipelines, evaluation scripts, even parts of the training stack. It doesn't replace the researcher, but it compresses the time between having an idea and seeing the experiment run. And in this field, iteration speed is almost everything. Whoever runs more good experiments per unit of time tends to win.

The second layer is data. For a long time, scaling meant more human data, more tokens from the internet. That well is finite. So increasingly the model participates in generating, filtering, and verifying its own training signal. In domains where you can check an answer, like math, code, or anything with a verifier, the model can explore, make mistakes, and learn from the ones that work. That's the reinforcement learning loop. The model is effectively teaching itself, and we are just designing the environment.

The third layer, which is still early, is research itself. Can the model propose hypotheses, read the literature, suggest which ablation to run next? Today it's more of a very good assistant than an independent scientist. But I don't think that gap stays wide for long.

So if you ask me where I personally benefit, it's that my job shifts. Less time on execution, more time on judgment. Deciding what matters, what to bet on, what question is worth the compute. The model handles more and more of the "how," and the humans are increasingly concentrated on the "what" and the "why." I think that's the healthy direction, and honestly it's the only way a small team can compete with much larger ones.

r001.rationale: The response says AI helps write code for infrastructure, data pipelines, and training tasks, but does not state that it removes lack of coding ability as a barrier to doing those tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think AI can help at two levels. One is making the research process faster—helping us write code, run experiments, analyze results, and understand why something didn’t work. That lets researchers spend more time on the questions that really matter.

The other level, which is more exciting, is helping us decide what to explore. Can AI propose a useful hypothesis or identify an assumption we should challenge? Research isn’t just about executing a plan efficiently; it’s also about finding the right direction.

I think we’ll move toward a tighter loop where humans and AI develop ideas together, test them, and learn from the results. But the ability to evaluate those ideas is crucial. Generating more ideas only helps if we can reliably tell which ones represent real progress.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can help researchers write code and run experiments faster, but does not state that it removes lack of coding ability as a barrier to model-training or data-processing tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI can help at almost every stage of research. It can help us read papers, write code, design experiments, and analyze results. That makes the feedback loop much faster: you have an idea, test it, understand what happened, and try again.

But the more interesting question is whether AI can help us discover something we wouldn’t have thought of ourselves. Can it propose a new hypothesis or find a flaw in how we’re framing a problem? That’s a bigger step than simply making existing work more efficient.

As those capabilities improve, I think our role shifts toward asking better questions and deciding which results to trust. You still need rigorous experiments. Generating more ideas is useful, but knowing which ideas actually work is what drives progress.
